Download the demonstration study →

Inspect the frozen protocol, original constructed records and six graph CSVs in an offline accessible report. The package includes a citation, release history and a draft museum pilot protocol.

Read accessible graph tables → · Read the museum pilot draft →


This public page explains the working prototype and how to use it. Screenshots show the actual interface with entirely constructed demonstration records. Research takes place in the separately run local application.

Experiment with this research tool

On request, I can send the GitHub repository or a copy of the tool itself. Describe your research interests and intended setting so we can identify a suitable starting point.

How existing studies and the public download are preserved

Templates create new drafts and identifiers. They do not install sample trials into your notebook or replace saved studies and locked protocol versions. The setup offers a way to restore the previous unsaved draft.

The downloadable demonstration study remains its original frozen 1.0.0 package. The practice fields illustrated above belong to current application exports; the older published ZIP has not been silently rebuilt.

Template questions and troubleshooting → Request the repository or tool →


For museums, galleries and curators


Give curatorial judgement an evidence trail.

For museums, galleries and curators who need to explain why a display, sequence or label was chosen and preserve the evidence behind that decision.

Every exhibition makes choices about what visitors encounter. If a decision is important enough to shape that encounter, it is important enough to leave a research record.


Museums and galleries

Bring a documented pilot into exhibition development, interpretation review and institutional research. Retain the alternatives, procedure and evidence alongside the eventual decision.


Curators and exhibition designers

Compare an arrangement, sequence or framing before committing to it. Make the question explicit, inspect what changed, and keep your judgement answerable to the record.


Learning, interpretation and visitor-research teams

Collect first accounts before showing an analysis, compare declared conditions, and retain observations, disagreements and exclusions for qualitative or mixed-method work.


Bring a real curatorial question.

Start with one decision your team is already discussing. These are proposed museum uses, illustrated with the working interface and constructed demonstration records.

Proposed museum workflow · interface illustration


Examine a label or curatorial framing

What changes when the same works are introduced differently?

A traceable comparison to bring into an interpretation review, with the texts, accounts and uncertainty retained.

How a museum team can use it

Retain two exact introductory texts as separate protocol conditions. Keep the works and presentation settings fixed. Collect first accounts before revealing the trace, then compare recorded interaction and code the written accounts.

When prior knowledge would defeat identity withholding, use a justified design with fresh participant groups. The app does not undo exposure to a label or automatically establish comprehension.

Proposed museum workflow · interface illustration


Test a pairing or display order

What does a different arrangement make available for comparison?

An inspectable basis for discussing a proposed pairing or sequence, including accounts that resist the curatorial premise.

How a museum team can use it

Keep the same artworks and use a linked reverse or rotation, or define the alternatives in a locked protocol. Review transitions, returns and first accounts by stable artwork identifier.

This is a digital comparison. Confirm decisions in the physical display; the tool does not reproduce gallery distance, lighting or visitor movement.

Proposed museum workflow · interface illustration


Develop a digital exhibition sequence

How does presenting works together differ from presenting them one at a time?

A documented pilot for a digital exhibition, collection presentation or facilitated looking session.

How a museum team can use it

Compare simultaneous and sequential conditions with declared durations, instructions and order. Inspect how presentation, selected time and written accounts differ; retain missing or interrupted trials.

Presentation and selection are separate measurements. A condition difference is descriptive until the study design supports a stronger inference.

Proposed museum workflow · interface illustration


Study the role of detail and magnification

Does a looking glass change recorded exploration and description?

A reproducible record for discussing detail access and close-looking exercises, with region definitions retained.

How a museum team can use it

Name image regions before collection. Compare clear and magnifying conditions using the same works, display and instructions. Review regional pointer dwell, entries and accounts alongside the lens settings.

Region membership follows the pointer centre. It is not eye tracking, and the lens itself changes the encounter.

Proposed museum workflow · interface illustration


Document a facilitated looking session

What do participants describe before the analysis invites an explanation?

Material for staff reflection, teaching and qualitative evaluation that preserves what was said at each stage.

How a museum team can use it

Retain an exact facilitation prompt, collect the first account, then keep later trace-assisted reflection separate. Use distinct coder codes when reviewing observation, self-report, inference and counterevidence.

Define an appropriate independent rubric if the question concerns learning or comprehension. The software does not generate a learning score or resolve coding disagreements.

Proposed museum workflow · interface illustration


Keep a curatorial decision record

Can another colleague inspect the evidence and the reach of the claim?

A research package a team can revisit, scrutinise and carry into a later display review.

How a museum team can use it

Link each claim to a work, region, interval, account or external source. State uncertainty and the reason for exclusions. Export the frozen protocol, records, annotations, images, tables and verification material.

The researcher writes and justifies the conclusion. File checks and retained revisions make scrutiny possible; they do not certify the curatorial judgement.


From a question to a curatorial review.

 1. Choose one decision
    
    Start with a real exhibition question: a framing, pairing, sequence or use of detail. Define the evidence that would inform it and the decision that remains a matter of judgement.

 2. Rehearse and lock the comparison
    
    Check the images, instructions, regions, input method and exports. Declare recruitment, allocation, exclusions and analysis before collection; then lock the version you intend to run.

 3. Run a consented pilot
    
    Use pseudonymous codes and the same declared procedure. Preserve first accounts, early stops and disagreements. Choose a justified recruitment size; the software supplies no universal sample size.

 4. Return to the curatorial meeting
    
    Set traces beside accounts and inspect the claim–evidence ledger. Record what the pilot supports, what remains uncertain, and what needs checking in the gallery. Keep the evidence package and recovery backup.


A record to bring into the curatorial meeting.

Keep the question and alternatives, a locked protocol, region definitions, participant accounts, recorded interaction, reasoned exclusions and claim–evidence annotations together. Export the records, tidy tables, source images and verification material so another colleague can inspect the reasoning.

Request it for your museum →Run the worked study →Read the research programme →

Tell Museum of One your institution or practice, the curatorial question and the intended setting. On request, I can send the GitHub repository or a copy of the tool itself.

Use it as a documented digital pilot. The current working prototype supports facilitated comparative studies with images. Pair it with appropriate recruitment, consent and an analysis plan, and check the transfer of any conclusion to a physical exhibition. Pointer interaction is not gaze, preference or proof of understanding.

Research is part of the museum role described in ICOM’s museum definition. Encounter Differential offers one practical way to make the investigation of a curatorial choice explicit and inspectable.

Run a study of your own.

Open the complete study guide & FAQ →

Individuals and institutions can request the GitHub repository or the tool itself. The website presents documentation and static images.

The export example retains eight completed demonstration trials plus one explicitly excluded scripted rehearsal. The participant comparison uses the eight completed trials. Integrity checks do not establish empirical validity.



What it does and what it can be used for

 * Built-in study templates: an editable demonstration comparison and museum feasibility pilot, with fresh identifiers, practice or research purpose, documented readiness review and one-condition-per-person pilot assignment.
 * Recorded practice: save and export rehearsals while keeping them outside participant cohorts; current trial tables explicitly retain practice status.
 * Protocol designer: versioned questions, conditions, instructions, allocation plans, stopping rules, exclusions and local design fingerprints.
 * Regions of interest: named image-coordinate polygons, pointer-centre dwell, entries, returns and lens-condition dwell.
 * Looking glass: transparent or magnifying viewing conditions retained with the interaction record; simultaneous and sequential presentations.
 * First accounts and evidence: description before analysis is revealed, then a claim–evidence ledger separating observation, self-report, inference and counterevidence.
 * Participant comparisons: exact-protocol cohorts, participant-level condition summaries, paired descriptive differences and explicit exclusions.
 * Preservation and export: a local notebook, revisions, recovery, acquisition manifests, evidence ZIPs with a dictionary and independent recomputation script, plus separate full-database backups.


Possible research uses include framing and label comparisons, magnification and display-condition pilots, sequence and adjacency experiments, close-description teaching, and qualitative coding of first accounts. Each use needs its own defensible design. The tool records interaction and accounts of an encounter; it does not decide what an artwork means or rate a viewer’s perception.



Post-Interpretive Criticism and aesthetics

The procedure makes the conditions of an encounter available for scrutiny and preserves a description before the trace invites explanation. For PIC, the useful distinction is between observable interaction, the participant’s account, the researcher’s inference and what remains unresolved. An unexpected or resistant account should remain evidence rather than be forced into a preferred interpretation. Withheld labels, the cursor and the lens also shape the encounter and belong in the analysis.



Worked study: Clear glass and magnification

Question: How does a 2× looking glass change recorded exploration and the participant’s description, compared with a clear 1× glass?

This is a design rehearsal, not an empirical finding. The four allocation rows illustrate counterbalancing and do not prescribe a sample size.

Hold the works, framing, input method and instructions constant.ConditionPresentationLabelsGlassActive timeClear glassTogether in one fieldWithheld1×60 secondsMagnifying glassTogether in one fieldWithheld2×60 seconds

Common instruction: Move the pointer naturally over the works. You may pause or stop at any time. Afterwards, describe what appeared before looking at the recorded trace.

Analysis plan: Exploratory within-participant comparison. Average repeated trials within participant and condition first. Compare per-work selected share of active time, paired differences, region pointer dwell and first accounts. Report missing, interrupted, early-stop and excluded trials, order, familiarity and lens reactivity. Do not infer gaze or aesthetic preference.

Stopping rule: 60 active seconds per condition. Participants may stop earlier or withdraw. Retain early exits and interrupted records; exclude rehearsal records with a stated reason. Declare recruitment size, eligibility and any further exclusions before collection.

Seed: lens-pilot-01. Allocation: Rotated and reversed counterbalancing. One repeat per condition.

Keep one participant’s code and allocation row across their conditions.Illustrative codeAllocation rowPlanned condition orderP0010Clear → MagnifyingP0021Magnifying → ClearP0032Magnifying → ClearP0043Clear → Magnifying



How to run the study

Inside the application, select How to use on the opening screen or Study guide & FAQ in setup. Opening the guide preserves the current setup.

 1. Define the question and evidence
 2. Compose the artworks and conditions
 3. Mark regions before collecting data
 4. Design and lock the protocol
 5. Assign and run participant trials
 6. Inspect the trace and document claims
 7. Compare participants and conditions
 8. Export the evidence and preserve the notebook


1. Define the question and evidence

Choose a question the instrument can actually address.

Read the procedure and research checks

Use Field studies for the full research workflow, even when you need only two artworks. The simpler paired encounter remains available as a separate, shorter flow.

The worked design below compares a clear 1× looking glass with a 2× magnifying glass. It concerns recorded interaction and accounts of an encounter. It cannot establish what someone saw, felt, preferred or understood.

Declare the intended unit of analysis, recruitment and sample-size rationale, repeated measures, exclusions, stopping rule and handling of missing data before collecting observations. A software default is not a power calculation. The four-row schedule is an allocation illustration, not a recommended or validated sample size.

Explain the procedure and intended data use to participants, obtain appropriate consent, choose pseudonymous codes, and keep any identity-to-code key outside this notebook. Decide who may see raw paths, writing and exports, and how long they will be retained.

Before continuing:

 * One specific question
 * A stated primary outcome and exploratory outcomes
 * Participant and data-handling plan
 * Declared sampling and exclusion rationale


2. Compose the artworks and conditions

Field studies → Create a field study.

See the interface example ↑

Read the procedure and research checks

Choose 2–8 distinct artworks. Use the bundled collection or images you are entitled to use. Record titles, artists, dates and source information, then choose presentation order. Uploaded images stay local and are not recompressed.

For the worked design, keep the same works, simultaneous presentation, identity-label setting, instruction and contextual framing in both conditions. Only the starting magnification changes from 1× to 2×. Record screen, room, lighting, sound and relevant prior familiarity as far as practicable.

Selecting or presenting a work is not a measure of gaze. Navigation in sequential mode records presentation; pointer or deliberate touch/keyboard selection records selected time. Keep input methods consistent when the question requires it.

Before continuing:

 * Works and rights checked
 * Identity and presentation settings reviewed
 * Exact instructions and framing retained
 * Device, input method and surrounding conditions recorded


3. Mark regions before collecting data

Expand Protocol designer & regions of interest; use the region editor first.

See the interface example ↑

Read the procedure and research checks

Choose the artwork in the region editor. Click at least three vertices around a meaningful part of the image, then enter a descriptive name and select Save region. Use Undo vertex or Clear drawing before saving. Crossed or degenerate polygons are rejected.

Keyboard users can focus the polygon editor, move the crosshair with arrow keys and press Enter to add a vertex. Name regions descriptively, such as “cypress grouping” or “open sky”, rather than naming an assumed psychological effect.

Coordinates refer to the image, not a particular screen size. Boundary points count as inside. Each polygon is scored independently: overlapping regions accrue overlapping time, so their totals must not be added as though they partition the image.

Region dwell follows the last observed pointer centre until the next observed position, leave, pause or end. Entries count transitions into a region; returns are entries after the first. Lens dwell and magnified dwell concern the pointer centre, not every pixel under the lens. Touch and keyboard selection do not invent a within-image pointer position.

Region definitions are frozen with acquisition. Do not redraw them after seeing results and describe that analysis as prespecified. Amend the protocol for future trials. Legacy records without these measurements remain explicitly incomplete.

Before continuing:

 * Regions named and saved on each relevant work
 * Overlaps intentional and disclosed
 * Definitions settled before looking at results


4. Design and lock the protocol

Complete the versioned protocol designer beneath the region editor.

See the interface example ↑

Read the procedure and research checks

Enter a protocol title, research question, seed, prespecified analysis plan, stopping/exclusion rules, recruitment notes and common participant instruction. Add each condition and its exact framing, instruction, presentation, identity visibility, cursor, magnification and active-time duration.

For the worked design, create Clear glass at 1× and Magnifying glass at 2×, both for 60 active seconds. Use one repeat per condition for the simplest rehearsal. Treat further repetitions as repeated observations of the same participant, not additional independent people.

Choose Fixed order, Seeded shuffle per allocation row, or Rotated and reversed counterbalancing. The latter rotates condition order and artwork position across rows and reverses condition order on alternate cycles; it is not a full Latin-square design. Inspect the planned order. In this two-condition example, artwork positions stay the same within a participant’s pair of conditions but can rotate across allocation rows.

Save protocol draft while developing the design. Lock protocol captures the current artworks and regions, versions the definition and records its SHA-256 fingerprint. Review the locked work/region counts and planned order before launch. Create amended version for any subsequent change; never silently combine versions in one comparison.

A local lock is an audit aid, not an external preregistration or independently certified timestamp. If the project needs preregistration, register the design through the appropriate separate process before collecting its data.

Before continuing:

 * Both conditions reviewed
 * Seed and allocation recorded
 * Analysis and stopping rules stated
 * Current artwork and region counts correct
 * Locked version and fingerprint retained


5. Assign and run participant trials

Use one stable participant code and a deliberate allocation row.

See the interface example ↑

Read the procedure and research checks

Enter P001 and allocation row 0, inspect the trial list, and select Run assigned trial. Use P002 with row 1 for the next participant, following your declared allocation plan. A participant’s code must stay the same across their conditions and repetitions. The app cannot establish who used a code.

Begin with a rehearsal. Use a clearly marked rehearsal code and record an explicit exclusion decision afterwards; do not count it as participant evidence. Check image loading, pointer/lens behaviour, timing, regions, instructions, first-account collection and exports before recruiting.

The participant reads the exact framing and instructions before Begin study encounter. In protocol mode, lens controls stay fixed and live counters are withheld. Pause and stop remain available. Images are withheld while paused; loss of focus or backgrounding pauses measurement and requires explicit resume.

Fixed-duration trials end at the active-time target; early manual stopping is recorded separately. Actual recorded duration remains in the log. Five-second checkpoints support interrupted-session recovery, which preserves the last committed trace and marks the encounter interrupted. The missing final interval is not reconstructed.

After each encounter, save the first descriptive account before opening analysis or revealing withheld identities. An empty account is also a recorded choice. The first account stays separate from later trace-assisted reflection. Continue to next assigned trial from the report. For a new participant, reopen the saved locked protocol and assign the next code/row; do not treat changing a code as an automatic new recruitment record.

Before continuing:

 * Code and allocation row correct
 * Rehearsal excluded with a reason
 * First account precedes analysis
 * Early stops and interruptions retained
 * Every planned trial accounted for


6. Inspect the trace and document claims

Set recorded events beside the participant’s account.

See the interface example ↑

Read the procedure and research checks

Explore per-work selected share, visits, returns, pointer paths, replay, regional maps, transitions and condition comparisons. Active time includes unassigned time; selected share is selected work time divided by total active time. Different exposure durations or input methods can change the comparison.

Inspect the region table for dwell, entries/returns, first entry and lens/magnified dwell. Inspect the measurement manifest for software/calculation versions, source-image checksums, viewport, actual rendered image geometry, sampling and interruptions. Missing acquisition information in legacy records has not been reconstructed.

Use the claim–evidence ledger to distinguish observation, self-report, inference and counterevidence. Give each entry a coder code, an evidence reference, uncertainty and, when relevant, an artwork, region and active-time interval. An account that disagrees with the trace is not automatically an error to correct.

For example, an observation may say “the pointer centre remained inside the cypress region for this interval”. “The participant preferred the tree” is an inference that this trace cannot establish. A participant’s own statement remains self-report, not a measured preference score.

Use Revise annotation when an entry changes. Earlier revisions remain inspectable. Under Analysis inclusion decision, state and save a reason for any exclusion; the original recording stays retained. Independent coders should use distinct codes and retain disagreements before any separate adjudication.

Before continuing:

 * Claim types distinguishable
 * Evidence and uncertainty explicit
 * Exclusions have reasons
 * First account preserved alongside later reflection


7. Compare participants and conditions

Field studies → Participant analysis.

See the interface example ↑

Read the procedure and research checks

Select one exact locked protocol version/hash. Filter by participant code or input method only when that matches the declared analysis. The input filter includes sessions that used that method; mixed-input sessions may still be present.

Completed trials with participant codes contribute by default; interrupted, early-stop and explicitly excluded records do not. Review included/excluded counts and repeated-assignment flags. Retakes remain visible rather than being silently discarded; inspect them and record any exclusion decision.

Repeated trials are averaged within participant and condition before the group descriptive mean is calculated. Each per-work row reports its own participant and trial counts, mean selected share and observed participant range. Zero-active-time trials cannot supply a selected-share value.

Within-participant differences include only people with both compared conditions. The displayed difference is second condition minus first in percentage points of selected share. It is descriptive and unadjusted for order, familiarity and other covariates; the app does not produce a significance test or a causal verdict.

The group panel summarizes per-work selected share. Inspect ROI dwell and written accounts in the individual records and exported tables, or use a separately specified external analysis. The interface does not automatically calculate cohort ROI effects, coder agreement, statistical power or eye-tracking validity.

Before continuing:

 * One exact protocol version
 * Independent participants counted correctly
 * Missing conditions and repeated assignments reviewed
 * Order, familiarity, input and lens reactivity reported
 * Descriptive findings kept separate from causal claims


8. Export the evidence and preserve the notebook

Use a research ZIP for analysis and a full database backup for recovery.

Read the procedure and research checks

In a study report, choose Export reproducible ZIP. In Participant analysis, Export selected trials & tidy tables exports the current selection. The bundle contains authoritative study JSON, frozen protocol definitions, region vertices, first accounts, later reflections, annotations, manifests, source images when retrievable, CSV tables, a data dictionary, checksums and a Python verification script.

Extract the ZIP into a folder. Run “python3 verify-and-recompute.py” from a terminal using that folder’s script. It checks bundled file hashes and recomputes complete work dwell and polygon dwell from the retained trace. A truncated legacy trace is reported rather than treated as a complete recomputation. This verifies selected software calculations, not scientific validity.

Review assets.json: exported images are compared with acquisition hashes when available. A later remote image can differ or become unavailable. Do not describe an unavailable or changed image as the verified original stimulus. CSV text that could execute as a spreadsheet formula is escaped; JSON preserves the exact text.

Use Database & recovery → Back up full database separately. That backup includes revisions, original-storage snapshots, images, removed records, conflicts and recovery drafts. A research ZIP is an analytical package, not the full database recovery archive.

IndexedDB commits locally; the SQLite mirror is a second local copy when connected. Check pending writes and mirror status. Browser and desktop origins have separate notebooks. Use an inspected full backup to transfer data. Keep a backup outside the working device, review sharing and rights, and do not publish raw participant writing or identifiers by accident.

Before continuing:

 * Correct records and filters exported
 * Dictionary and manifests retained
 * Checksums and recomputation reviewed
 * Changed/unavailable images disclosed
 * Full database backup stored separately
 * Sharing reviewed before release



FAQ and troubleshooting

How do I start from a demonstration or museum pilot template?

Open Field studies → Use a study template, then choose a template. It opens a separate draft with a new identifier; no demonstration trials are imported. Review the works and regions, intended use and readiness notes. Save the draft, lock it, then enter a participant code and allocation row to run the assigned trial. Saved protocols remain available under Saved protocol. Restore previous setup returns to the earlier unsaved setup while this view stays open.

How do practice and participant research differ?

The demonstration template starts in Practice only. Your own practice encounters are saved and exportable, but excluded from participant cohorts, including recovery checkpoints and linked variations. They are different from the synthetic analysis-lab example. To adapt a template for participant research, choose that intended use and complete every readiness item with notes before locking. That local review is not ethics approval or external preregistration.

Why does the museum pilot assign only one framing to a person?

The draft proposes parallel arms. Its seeded schedule assigns one condition per allocation row, balanced in blocks of four for two conditions, and keeps work positions fixed. Use one unique participant code and row per person, retain the seed and concealed allocation under a custodian, and apply the proposed 24-person stopping rule yourself. The demonstration instead assigns both lens conditions to each person.

What is the tool’s current status, and how can I experiment with it?

Encounter Differential is a working prototype maintained by Museum of One. Individuals and institutions interested in experimenting with it can contact research@museumofone.art to request the GitHub repository or a copy of the tool. Its public website provides documentation and screenshots. Software checks do not establish empirical validity.

Is the looking glass eye tracking?

No. It records pointer-centre position and interface interaction. A pointer can be parked while someone looks elsewhere. Gaze claims require a separately calibrated method and a validation study for the actual task.

Can I run a research protocol with only two artworks?

Yes. Use Field studies and remove works until two remain. The shorter paired-encounter flow has different controls; use the field-study workflow for locked protocols, polygon regions, first accounts and participant comparisons.

Can I change artworks, regions or settings after locking?

Create an amended protocol version for future trials. The locked design and acquired recording remain unchanged. Reflections, evidence annotations and inclusion decisions create revisions without changing the raw recording.

What does selected share mean?

Selected work time divided by active session time, including unassigned active time. It is a percentage of recorded interaction time, not a probability of preference or a percentage of time spent looking.

Why do region totals exceed work time?

Overlapping polygons are scored independently. Overlapping time can belong to more than one region. Region sums are not a partition unless the regions were designed to be mutually exclusive.

Does a larger lens measure its whole footprint?

No. Region membership uses the pointer centre. Lens dwell and magnified dwell record the viewing condition at that point; they do not measure everything visible through the circular lens.

How do I resume another day?

Reopen the saved locked protocol, keep the same participant code and allocation row for that participant, and select the intended next trial from the planned list. Check existing records first to avoid accidental duplicate assignments. Interrupted checkpoints recover the last committed trace; they do not resume a supposedly continuous encounter.

Why is a record absent from Participant analysis?

Check the exact protocol version/hash, code and input filters, completion status and saved inclusion decision. Legacy/ad hoc records without a locked protocol remain in the notebook but do not join this protocol comparison. Missing paired conditions exclude that person from that particular paired difference.

Are pauses or early stops discarded?

No. Paused time remains separate from active time. Early-stop and interrupted records remain retained and are excluded from the default completed-trial cohort. State how such records will be handled before collecting data.

Are local protocol locks equivalent to preregistration?

No. They preserve the local version and fingerprint. External registration, independent timing evidence and a declared analysis process are separate research practices.

Which export should I keep?

Keep both: a reproducible ZIP for the selected analytical evidence, and a full database backup for the notebook, revisions and recovery records. A CSV alone does not preserve the whole situation.

Do the validation checks validate PIC or a measure of attention?

No. The Validation register runs scripted software reference checks and outlines empirical work still needed: timing/device replication, lens reactivity, calibrated-gaze comparisons where relevant, coding reliability and test–retest/usability. No human validation result is supplied by a passing benchmark.

Does this website run the app or collect study material?

No. The public Museum of One page is documentation with static demonstration screenshots. It contains no app embed, participant upload form, executable study, or downloadable app installer. Study work remains in the separately run local application.



About the images and export examples

The fifteen-image visual tour shows the actual interface in an isolated documentation notebook, alongside readable previews derived from its exported files. The traces, participant codes, accounts and comparisons were constructed for explanation. They contain no private study records and report no participant findings. Artworks shown are from the public-domain Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access collection, with source records retained in the tool.

The evidence-package example contains eight completed demonstration trials and one excluded scripted rehearsal. Cohort summaries use the eight completed trials. Export previews retain the actual file names, values and independent verification output; they are labelled as readable previews rather than application screens.



Scope and limits

A pointer trace is not gaze. Selected time is not preference. Region definitions and lens settings influence what is measured. Overlapping regions cannot be summed as a partition. Comparisons are descriptive and do not provide inferential tests, causal estimates or automatic coder agreement. Local protocol locking is not external preregistration. The Validation register distinguishes software reference checks from empirical studies still needed.

Use pseudonyms, appropriate consent, an explicit sampling rationale and a declared analysis plan. Review writing, stimulus rights and identifiers before sharing an export. Keep full recovery backups separately from evidence packages.



Citation and revision

08 Canon of Witnesses - The Language of the Crack: On Doris Salcedo’s Shibboleth Doris Salcedo’s Shibboleth isn’t an installation. It’s a rupture. Architectural, historical, and ethical. Dorian Vale


Museum of One, Independent Research Institute for Contemporary Aesthetics


Written at the Threshold




Doris Salcedo’s Shibboleth (2007) isn’t an installation. It’s a rupture. Architectural, historical, and ethical. Commissioned for the Turbine Hall of Tate Modern in 2007, the work unveiled a 167-meter crack carved directly into the museum’s concrete floor, as if a wound had opened inside the institution itself.

Its form was serpentine, jagged, and unpredictable. In some places, it was barely wide enough to catch a coin; in others, wide enough to swallow a child’s foot. But it was not merely a disruption of physical space. It was a disruption of inherited narratives, institutional stability, and the illusion of cultural coherence. The floor, which normally represents a museum’s foundation, both literally and symbolically, was here turned into evidence.

The first time you encounter the crack, it doesn’t appear crafted. It appears accidental. As though the museum has ruptured under the weight of its own certainty. It’s too irregular to be part of the design, too defiant to be explained away. It runs like a scar across the floor of the Turbine Hall: uneven, erratic, unapologetic. It doesn’t trace a pattern. It tears one.

Visitors don’t merely see the crack. They hesitate. Some stepped over it briskly, mistaking rupture for ornament. Others linger, crouch, tilt their heads, as though nearness might translate silence into sense. A few avert their gaze entirely, as one does when grief arrives without invitation or name. But none, not even the critics armed with footnotes and euphemisms, can pretend it is not there.

This is no object awaiting admiration. This is a wound, deliberate, disobedient, carved into the cathedral that once promised to keep culture intact.

Shibboleth is perhaps Salcedo’s most publicly invasive work. A literal breach in the foundation of one of the world’s most self-assured art spaces. The crack didn’t decorate the Turbine Hall; it divided it. It carved its way through the floor and through the viewer’s assumption of architectural trust. Some parts were shallow, others gaping. There was no consistency. And that was the point.

Salcedo didn’t install an artwork. She violated a building. The first sensation isn’t aesthetic. It’s bodily. Your gait shifts. Your posture changes. Your muscles hold the low-grade alertness of something being “off.” The architecture, once assumed whole, is now unpredictable. The viewer begins to walk with doubt. And it’s here that Salcedo’s genius quietly detonates. What she fractures is not merely the concrete, but the authority of the institution to frame violence in neutral tones.

The word shibboleth refers to a biblical test. A linguistic password that separated insiders from outsiders. Those who mispronounced it were killed. The difference was phonetic, not moral. A simple inflection meant the difference between belonging and annihilation. In choosing this word as her title, Salcedo transforms the work into a test of its own: who recognizes the violence, and who walks over it unfazed?

And yet, she never spells this out. There’s no wall text pointing toward colonialism, immigration, or racial exclusion, though all of these haunt the work. She offers no verbal script. Instead, she invites misreading. She tempts the viewer to aestheticize the scar, to flatten its trauma into motif, and in doing so, revealing their preference for theory over truth.

Salcedo’s refusal to interpret the work isn’t vagueness. It’s discipline. She refuses to grant the institution the final word. The crack isn’t explained. It’s endured. It’s the physical manifestation of every invisible line society has drawn between the “civilized” world and the bodies it has cost. And here, unmistakably, she aligns with the ethic of Post-Interpretive Criticism.

She does not illustrate grief. She builds with its residue. She doesn’t translate trauma. She embeds it untranslated, into structure.  And in doing so, she removes the viewer’s comfort, of altitude, of the luxury to hover above the scene unscathed.

Shibboleth appears passive at first. But to stand beside it is to feel its violence. There is nothing theatrical about it. It’s dangerous. Children could fall in. Heels could catch. Wheelchairs must divert. It’s not a simulation of injury. It’s a real architectural breach. And that reality is what makes it sacred. Salcedo returns consequence to the gallery floor. She makes the act of walking, once passive, a moral reckoning.

When Shibboleth was de-installed, if you dares to call the burial of a wound a “de-installation”, the museum sealed the crack. The concrete was patched. The floor repainted. But it wasn’t erased. A faint scar remains. Discolored. Disobedient. A quiet defiance against the institution’s desire for architectural amnesia.

This scar isn’t a memory. It’s a refusal to forget.

Most institutions commemorate trauma by encasing it. By sealing the wound in plaque and poetry. Salcedo does not commemorate. Sh leaves it open. She refuses smooth history. She refuses the elegance of a metaphor.

The crack does not stand for something. It is something. It’s not symbolic. It’s literal. And when the museum sealed it, it wasn’t an act of healing. It was an act of forgetting. And sealing isn’t meant to heal, it’s to silence.

To see the scar now requires moral alertness. More than vision. It demands moral alertness, a kind of ethical hearing. A readiness to remember that something once split this space. That something made the building tremble. And that the institution, for all its power, couldn’t make the floor forget, and that it couldn’t be entirely erased.

In this, she doesn’t merely exemplify the doctrine of Post-Interpretive Criticism; she prefigures it. She offers no language, only structure and architecture. She doesn’t decorate pain. She disciplines space. Her work demands not interpretation, but restraint. Not commentary, but moral proximity.

And it’s precisely because of this, because she asks the viewer not to speak, but to stay, that she stands as the right name inscribed into the Canon of Witnesses. She doesn’t illustrate the theory. She enacts it. She injures the institution with the rigor of one who knows that silence, when applied with discernment, can be more honest than any speech.

When a work carries residue rather than message, when it refuses to be named without distortion, the critic’s duty is to hold the silence, not to fill it. Salcedo gives us this lesson in concrete. Shibboleth isn’t just a crack in the floor. It’s a mark of what can’t be sealed. It’s a wound that refused to become past tense.

She didn’t create a sculpture.

She scarred a foundation so that the world would remember what it tries so hard to forget.

By Deror_avi - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0



Museum of One, Written at the Threshold, 2025

The Journal of Post-Interpretive Criticism Open-access serial published by Museum of One Press, with numbered volumes, founder-led editorial review, and work-specific publication and rights records. The Journal of Post-Interpretive Criticism is an open-access serial published by Museum of One through the Museum of One Press imprint. It publishes theoretical essays, research documents, applied criticism, and edited exchanges concerned with Post-Interpretive Criticism and adjacent questions in aesthetics.

The Journal is published irregularly rather than on a fixed issue calendar. Its numbered volumes are editorially assembled releases within the serial. The ISSN identifies the continuing journal; an ISBN identifies a particular book-format volume edition; a DOI identifies a specific repository release or version. Separately issued Museum of One Press books are listed in the Publication Register and are not journal volumes unless their own record says so.


Editorial arrangements and review

Editorial selection, editing, production, metadata, and corrections are currently handled by Dorian Vale, the publishing name of Tarique, for Museum of One Press. Dialogues and contributed exchanges are published with the knowledge or approval of their named participants.

The Journal does not currently operate a standing anonymous or external peer-review system. Unless an individual publication states otherwise, work is editorially reviewed rather than formally peer reviewed. Review includes factual and bibliographic consistency, source and quotation checks, contributor descriptions, rights and image credits, identifiers, and version information. Repository deposits, catalogue records, and indexing services improve preservation or discoverability; they do not constitute peer review or endorsement.


Published volumes


Volume I: Post-Interpretive Criticism: The Foundational Essays

Author: Dorian Vale
ISBN: 978-1-0698203-0-3
Serial: The Journal of Post-Interpretive Criticism, ISSN 2819-7232
Publisher: Museum of One, Canada; Museum of One Press imprint

This volume gathers the foundational doctrines, theoretical proposals, and applications of Post-Interpretive Criticism, including work on restraint, presence, and the responsibility of criticism.

Repository release and download, Zenodo · Volume I record


Volume II: Post-Interpretive Criticism: Essays from the Field

Author: Dorian Vale
ISBN: 978-1-0698203-1-0
Serial: The Journal of Post-Interpretive Criticism, ISSN 2819-7232
Publisher: Museum of One, Canada; Museum of One Press imprint

Volume II applies the framework through critical encounters with artists and works, including Araya Rasdjarmrearnsook, Kimsooja, Doris Salcedo, and Hiwa K.

Repository release and download, Zenodo · Volume II record


Volume III: Post-Interpretive Criticism: Canon of Witnesses

Subtitle: Fieldwork in Post-Interpretive Criticism
Author: Dorian Vale
ISBN: 978-1-0698203-2-7
Serial: The Journal of Post-Interpretive Criticism, ISSN 2819-7232
Publisher: Museum of One, Canada; Museum of One Press imprint

Volume III gathers twelve essays organized as applications of Post-Interpretive Criticism. The collection examines witnessing, restraint, and the ethical limits of critical language through individual encounters with artists’ practices.

Repository release and download, Zenodo · Volume III record


Publication records, rights, and corrections

The Journal’s serial identifier is ISSN 2819-7232. Its serial catalogue record is OCLC 1545514536, and its authority record is Wikidata Q136530009. Individual books, editions, and articles retain their own identifiers.

Original publication dates and later repository release or revision dates are distinct. The linked edition and repository record should be consulted for the date and version being cited. Cover designs and catalogue titles may differ; specific discrepancies are noted beside the relevant volume.

Reuse is governed by the licence stated on the individual work or edition. Copyright in third-party images or other material remains subject to its own rights notice. A site-level copyright statement does not override a work-level licence.

The Ethical Charter sets out research, editorial, attribution, access, and correction principles. Publisher details appear in the Publisher Imprint. Publication and correction enquiries: research@museumofone.art.


Selected writing

 * Canon of Witnesses: Araya Rasdjarmrearnsook
 * On Christian Boltanski and the Rituals of Loss
 * On Yoko Ono and the Violence of Interpretation
 * On Agnus by Konstantin Korobov (2022)
 * On Clouded Water: The Changing of Kok River
 * The Cult of the Medium – When Process Becomes Propaganda
 * Duchamp Made the First Cut: This Is the Second

See the Publication Register for separately issued books and the Dialogues for published exchanges.

Diagnostics Without Possession: An Operational Manual for Post-Interpretive Criticism (Operational reference for inter-rater reliability) A coding reference for the ten Post-Interpretive Criticism indices, covering coding units, exclusion rules, composite reporting and inter-rater reliability procedures. Includes contextual limits and provisional reliability targets. Research record and citation

Status: Published operational manual


Research summary

An operational reference for ten diagnostic indices, specifying coding units, inclusion and exclusion rules, contextual interpretation, composite reporting, and reliability procedures.

Research question: How can the framework’s indices be applied and reported consistently across coders?

Approach and sources: A coding manual covering Layer A ethical and postural indices and Layer B phenomenological fidelity indices, with workflow and reporting guidance.

Contribution: Makes coding choices, conventions, reliability targets, and operational extensions explicit for comparative work and critical self-audit.

Scope and limits: Reliability targets are provisional. Pilot agreement does not substitute for formal statistics; contextual sensitivity, cultural specificity, and interpretive irreducibility remain material limits.


Related research programmes

 * Phenomenological Methods and Diagnostic Reading: Published operational manual in this programme.


Publication history and rights

Publication record: Bibliographic year: 2026. Museum of One web record published 2026-05-09; current text updated 2026-10-14. Web timestamps do not establish the date of an earlier or separately deposited version.

Rights: Rights follow the notice attached to the individual work or edition. Consult the published text or repository record.


Cite this work

Dorian Vale. Diagnostics Without Possession: An Operational Manual for Post-Interpretive Criticism (Operational reference for inter-rater reliability). 2026. Museum of One Press. https://www.museumofone.art/diagnostics-without-possession-an-operational-manual-for-post-interpretive-criticism-operational-reference-for-inter-rater-reliability/

BibTeX · RIS · CSL JSON

This research summary was added on 14 October 2026 from the linked public text and bibliographic record. The complete argument, examples, and references remain in the published work.





























Dorian Vale


Museum of One, Independent Research Institute for Contemporary Aesthetics


Written at the Threshold





Purpose and Scope

This manual operationalizes the ten diagnostic indices of Post-Interpretive Criticism (PIC) for consistent application across coders. It supports inter-rater reliability work, comparative corpus studies, and self-audit by individual critics. It is a coding reference, not a theoretical exposition; the foundational arguments are set out in the published essays and are not rehearsed here except where required for operational clarity.

The manual covers two layers.

 * Layer A, Ethical / Postural Indices: RD, ILI, VDR, EPS, IAI. These diagnose how much force a critical text applies and where.
 * Layer B, Phenomenological Fidelity Indices: EFI, PPAS, RERR, QSARI, DCI. These diagnose which phenomenological operations the text honours or violates.

The two layers are separately tabulated and reported. Where they appear to diverge on the same phenomenological principle, divergences are reported, not averaged away.


How to Use This Manual

 1. Read Part I before coding any text. The general principles, coding units, Direction of Force, exclusion rules, the zero-denominator convention, and the PIC Constraint, apply to every index.
 2. Code Layer A first. Layer A produces a basic postural reading and supplies values needed for Layer B interpretation.
 3. Code Layer B second. Begin with the EFI procedural gate; if EFI falls in the Low band, the remaining Layer B profile is provisionally non-diagnostic for phenomenological fidelity until bracketing is reassessed.
 4. Assemble a composite profile rather than an aggregate score. Report all ten indices, posture classifications for each layer, and any divergences.
 5. Apply the PIC Constraint at every stage of interpretation. No index is read in isolation; no profile is read without genre awareness.


Foundational Sources

This manual is consistent with the following published v.2 specifications:

 * Vale, Dorian. Measuring Proximity: A Post-Interpretive Diagnostic Experiment in Art Criticism (Post-Hermeneutic Phenomenology) v.2. Museum of One, 2026. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18155622.
 * Vale, Dorian. From Husserl's Mathematics to Dufrenne's Aesthetics: Toward a Formalization of Phenomenological Aesthetics v.2. Museum of One, 2026. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18205916.
 * Vale, Dorian. Extending Post-Interpretive Criticism: Additional Diagnostic Indices for Enhanced Phenomenological Fidelity in Art Criticism v.2. Museum of One, 2026. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18498483.

Where this manual specifies operational rules not stated explicitly in the source essays, those specifications are derived directly from the essays' definitions and are flagged as operational extensions.


Part I: General Coding Principles


1.1 Coding Units

Different indices use different coding units. Apply the unit specified for each index without substitution.



Index

Coding unit

Notes

RD

Sentence

Devices counted per sentence; one device per occurrence.

ILI

Phrasal instance

Each interpretive or encounter-based claim coded once at the level of its functional phrase.

VDR

Phrasal instance

As ILI; coded for displacement vs. presence.

EPS

Phrasal instance

Restraint markers and closure assertions counted at the phrasal level.

IAI

Scored qualitatively across the passage; optional supplemental ratio for corpus work only.

EFI

Clause

Each clause counted once according to its dominant function.

PPAS

Statement

Each phase-relevant statement assigned to P1, P2, or P3.

RERR

Residue mention

Discrete references to Stillmark / Hauntmark or their equivalents.

QSARI

Statement

Statements assigning agency to or extracting agency from the artwork.

DCI

Clause (Phase 3-relevant)

Counts circulatory terms or oscillatory markers per clause; multiple markers in one clause count once.



Where a single sentence contains multiple clauses or phrasal instances, code each unit separately. Where a clause is split across sentences (e.g., by a dash or semicolon), treat each as a clause if it carries an independent function.


1.2 Direction of Force

All Layer A semantic coding is governed by a single orienting principle: the Direction of Force a unit applies. Units either drive the text toward interpretive closure or toward sustained encounter. The matrices below formalise the distinction.

1.3 Inclusion and Exclusion Rules

Across all indices, the following content types are excluded from numerator and denominator unless explicitly relevant:

 * Bibliographic and citation material (titles, dates, page numbers, references in running text).
 * Biographical or curriculum-vitae statements about the artist that do not bear on the encounter (“Trained at the Slade, 1991–1994”).
 * Administrative or institutional metadata (acknowledgements, funding statements, dimensions, materials lists, exhibition history).
 * Quoted material from third parties, unless the critic endorses or embeds the quotation as their own claim. When endorsed, code the embedded claim under the index it activates.
 * Headings, captions, and figure labels.

Inclusion is determined by functional relevance to the index, not by sentence length or grammatical completeness.


1.4 Zero-Denominator Convention

Any index whose denominator equals zero is recorded as N/A and excluded from composite means rather than forced to zero. N/A is reported with the reason for non-applicability.

 * EFI: PDS + PAS = 0.
 * PPAS: no phase statements present.
 * RERR: RMR + RMC = 0 (record “Residue Not Engaged” flag).
 * QSARI: QSS + QSO = 0.
 * DCI: TRC = 0.

The N/A convention prevents the absence of a phenomenon from being read as its failure. A text that does not engage residue is not a low-restraint text; it is a text outside the residue domain.


1.5 Rounding Convention

All ratio-based indices are rounded to two decimal places before band assignment. Apply rounding only at the reporting stage, not during intermediate calculations.


1.6 Genre Awareness

PIC profiles are read with awareness of the text's genre: short review, catalogue essay, academic monograph, artist statement, manifesto, lecture transcript, blog entry, social-media post. Different genres legitimately deploy different linguistic strategies; a high IAI in a museum catalogue carries different weight than a high IAI in a personal essay. Where validation studies are run, normalise by text length and document genre baselines.


1.7 The PIC Constraint

No index may be interpreted independently of at least two others, and no profile may be read without contextual genre awareness.

This is the governing interpretive rule of the framework. Single-index readings are never reported as posture diagnoses. A high RD score does not constitute Poetic posture; a low EPS does not constitute Colonising posture. Postures emerge from index combinations read against genre context.


1.8 Reliability Targets

For categorical classifications, including Layer A postures (Forensic, Colonising, Poetic, Institutionalist) and Layer B postures (Witness-Aligned, Extractive, Institutionally Overdetermined, Unstable), apply Cohen's κ. The provisional target is κ ≥ 0.80.

For continuous index values (RD₁₀₀, ILI, VDR, EPS, EFI, PPAS, RERR, QSARI, DCI), apply ICC (intraclass correlation coefficient). The provisional target is ICC ≥ 0.85.

Reliability statistics are reported alongside any comparative claim. Provisional pilot reliability (e.g., observed agreement on pattern detection) does not substitute for formal κ and ICC calculation in empirical work.


Part II: Layer A: Ethical / Postural Indices

Layer A indices answer the diagnostic question: how much force does this criticism apply, and where?


2.1 Rhetorical Density (RD)


Definition

RD quantifies the concentration of rhetorical devices per unit of text. It tracks linguistic pressure: how much force language applies to the encounter. RD is morally neutral. High RD is ethically permissible only when paired with low ILI, low VDR, and high EPS.


Coding unit

Sentence. Devices are tallied per sentence; one device per occurrence. Measurement is normalised by word count.


Calculation

RD = D / W    where D = number of rhetorical devices, W = total word count

RD₁₀₀ = (D / W) × 100    devices per 100 words

Compute over the full text or, for distribution analysis, over 200–500-word segments or 300-word windows at the beginning, middle, and end of the text.


Devices counted

 * Metaphor, figurative substitution where one term is used in place of another (“the wound of the canvas”).
 * Simile, explicit comparison using “like” or “as” (“the surface like rain on slate”).
 * Personification, attribution of human qualities to non-human subjects (“the geometry grows tired”).
 * Parallelism, matched grammatical structure across two or more clauses (“without certainty. Without demand.”).
 * Anaphora and epistrophe, repetition of the same word(s) at the beginning (anaphora) or end (epistrophe) of successive clauses.
 * Antithesis, pairing of contrasting ideas in parallel structure (“not inspiration but initiation”).
 * Rhetorical question, a question posed for effect, not for answer.
 * Aphorism, a compressed, sententious statement with the structure of a maxim (“Mercy doesn't need metaphor”).
 * Intensifier cluster, three or more intensifying modifiers in close sequence (“utterly, devastatingly, irreducibly given”).


Devices excluded

 * Plain adjectives serving descriptive function only.
 * Repetition for clarity or reference (e.g., reiteration of a proper noun).
 * Line breaks, bullet points, and other typographic devices.
 * Standard idioms that no longer carry figurative weight (“at first glance”).


Counting rules

 1. Count one device per occurrence. A single sentence may contain multiple devices; count each.
 2. If a phrase qualifies under more than one device category (e.g., a metaphor embedded in a parallel structure), count it under each category once. The functional analysis recovers compound effect.
 3. Sustained metaphors across multiple sentences are counted at each instance of figurative work, not as a single extended device.


Behavioural bands



RD₁₀₀

Band

Profile

PIC posture (when read with other indices)

0–2.99

Minimal

Forensic description

High restraint; risk of sterility

3–6.99

Descriptive–Analytical

Light figurative use

Careful interpretive zone

7–10.99

Expressive Control

Balanced rhetoric

Ethical if ILI and VDR remain low

11–15.99

Compressed Vigilance

Compressed rhetorical weight

Poetic witness zone

16–20.99

Performative

Borderline; classify by EPS and IAI

21+
